coverage.notes: Format is rated high for the FORMAL LAB REPORT only, on two instructor sources that agree: the Week 10 lab assignment, whose Appendix A is the Engineering Department Report Standards, and the instructor's report template. It does not cover the other two families. For the short-form reports (op-amp and active-filter labs) the assignments list what the report must contain, but the blank templates they point to were not found, so typography and page layout are unspecified. For the weekly digital-logic worksheets each handout states what to hand in, but the page layout is the handout's own. Methods and assignments are partial. Absence claims in this pack describe one search, not the world: all seven term folders of the student's iCloud archive and his university OneDrive, searched by course number and file name in September 2026. The report template the pack rests on is a student-saved copy (its metadata gives 2025-04-08, one revision, one minute of editing) with no student content. Its guidance sentences appear word for word in a second, partly student-written file, and its placeholders, company field, and text point to the instructor, but it cannot be shown to be byte-identical to the original. A file in the iCloud term folder that is named as the SP24 template is not the template: it is a student's draft saved over it, and no rule rests on its student pages. The only completed formal report found is a student's own, written in a complaint register; a near-identical copy is named as the assignment prescribes, but nothing shows it was submitted or graded, so it supports layout only and is not a model of prose or tone. The two short-form reports appear to be filled-in copies of the instructor's short-form templates (their file metadata credits the instructor, and the filter report's table rows cite the assignment's own step numbers), so their layout is probably the instructor's, and their prose is not a model. The printed instructor text on the weekly turn-in pages is extractable and was read for what to hand in. The weekly handout PDFs for weeks 1, 2, 3, 4 (both parts) and 6 in the iCloud term folder also carry the student's own answers, written in digital ink on the handout pages; all 62 of those pages were read as page images in September 2026, and what they show is recorded on the worksheet family as observed student practice, never as a requirement. One page carries what appears to be staff initials beside the handout's printed sign-off step; no page carries a score, a grade or written feedback, so what earned credit on a worksheet is still not shown. The PSpice homework and Quartus project files are tool output with no prompts or answers, and no rule rests on them. No syllabus, rubric, test, or answer key for the lab was found in that search; the lab has weekly worksheets and reports, and no tests.

course_policy.summary: No syllabus or generative-AI policy for this course was found in a search of all seven term folders of the student's iCloud archive and his university OneDrive, by course number, in September 2026. By the student's instruction an archived syllabus is treated as outdated and is not mined, so one that turned up would be excluded. The current policy is unknown: ask the student to confirm it with the instructor.

format.deliverable: formal engineering lab report (analog labs); short-form lab report (design-project labs). The other format nodes state rules for the formal report only; the short-form reports and the weekly worksheets are described in their own family nodes.
precedence: the specific lab assignment and its report steps (for the formal report, the Week 10 assignment)
the instructor's report template, including the guidance text inside it
Appendix A of that assignment, the Engineering Department Report Standards

page.margin_note: At least 1 inch on every side; figures and tables stay inside the margins, and nothing is written in the margins.
page.source: Stated for the formal report only: Appendix A + instructor template

typography.paragraph_separation: Every paragraph break is visible: either an indented first line or an extra blank line.
typography.large_table_exception: In appendices, a smaller font is acceptable to keep a wide table on one page if it stays legible.
typography.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template + Appendix A (double spacing)

title_page.source: Stated for the formal report only: Appendix A (title, author, date, class, professor) + instructor template (experiment partner line). Lab section is listed in neither; the file-naming rule uses the section letter and the observed reports show it.

abstract.placement: the instructor template allows the abstract on its own page or on the title page. Own page after the title page is the safe default: it is what the observed report does and it keeps the title page uncluttered.
abstract.length: one short paragraph (department standard). The instructor template allows one or two very short paragraphs, no more than 6-8 sentences in all.
abstract.content: brief introduction, the kinds of experiments performed, and a summary of results without detailed numeric data. An abstract is not an introduction: it summarizes the whole report.
forbidden: references to figures or tables, because the reader may not have the rest of the report in front of them
abstract.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template + Appendix A

page_numbering.appendices: same margin and numbering rules as the body
page_numbering.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template

body.section_numbering: outline style built with Word heading styles (1., 1.1, and deeper if needed). The template's own sections use two levels. A third level (1.2.1) appears in a student's report; 'up to three levels' is not a limit either source states.
sections_template: 1.2 Second Section Title (the template leaves this title to the author; a student's report used Background and Context)
body.sections_note: The template's sections are a model. Different sections are acceptable when the author has a clear reason for them and can best communicate with the reader that way. The template's second introduction section holds background theory, equations, and diagrams of the system.
body.section_openers: Every section starts with a leading paragraph that introduces it, and the introduction previews the subsections that follow.
body.subsections: A section that has subsections has at least two.
body.length: Should not exceed about 8-10 written pages. The strongest reports run about 5 pages of text, excluding graphs, sketches, and tables.
body.no_flipping: Figures necessary to follow the analysis stay in the body, not the appendices, so a reader does not flip back and forth. Pictures and graphs go where they are discussed.
body.writing_for_the_reader: Write so that another student with the same educational background could duplicate the results. Use equations for mathematical relationships. Be precise about which quantity is meant: label a voltage with a polarity on the circuit diagram and name it (for example, V_R1 measured with the oscilloscope probe), not 'the voltage was measured'.
body.procedure_section: Experimental Procedure reports what happened, so a reader could repeat it, and does not tell the reader what to do. The equipment section is not a bare list: it says why each instrument was needed. Simulations and other model checks go under Other Verification Methods, naming the tools.
body.results_section: Present all recorded data, measured, theoretical, and simulated. Use graphs to show trends unless the data set is very small, and move large tables to an appendix with a reference in the text.
body.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template (section names, lead paragraphs, subsections, procedure and results guidance) + Appendix A (required elements, length, no flipping, writing for the reader)

equations.placement: in the body, carried over from the pre-lab work (the Week 9 handout says they may be included directly, and the Week 10 assignment says to paste them into the main part of the report)
equations.size_rule: A small equation may sit inside a sentence. If the line spacing changes to fit it, treat it as large: center it between the margins and set it off with white space.
equations.numbering_observed: The Week 9 pre-lab template labels equations Equation N and the handout cites them as Eq. N. The formal-report template does not say whether to number them; a student's report did.
equations.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template (equation editor, size rule) + Week 9 and Week 10 assignments

figures.caption_pattern: Figure N. Descriptive title. A caption must stand alone, so 'Figure 3. Flow Tube Setup', not 'Figure 3' and not 'Flow Tube Setup'.
figures.numbering: sequential, in the order first cited
figures.text_reference: Every figure and table is cited in the text, and the citation comes before the figure or table it points to.
figures.naming: If a thing cannot be called a table, call it a figure, not a diagram or a picture.
plot_rules: no title text inside the graph; the caption titles it, so an Excel graph title is removed
measured data as markers only (circles, squares, triangles), not connected by lines
simulation and equation data as smooth lines with no markers (solid, dashed, dotted)
every axis labeled with variable and units
logarithmic frequency axis for frequency sweeps
axis limits matched to the data range
distinguishable in black-and-white print, since colors mostly are not
traces that exactly overlap are acceptable; say so when describing the graph
figures.prelab_exception: The Week 9 pre-lab turn-in asks for graphs 'properly titled with legends', and its example graphs carry titles. The no-title rule applies to graphs in the formal report, where the caption is the title.
figures.schematics: circuit diagrams from PSpice pasted into the body as captioned figures (pasting as a picture works best). Sketches drawn with CAD tools are preferred to hand sketches because they are embedded in the document.
figures.source: Stated for the formal report only: Week 10 assignment + Appendix A part IV + instructor template

tables.caption_pattern: Table N. Descriptive title, standing alone the way a figure caption does
rules: display precision set to a reasonable number of significant digits; ordinary notation is preferred over scientific when it stays readable
cited in the text before the table appears, and placed in the order cited
a very large table goes in an appendix with a reference in the text
a list table may hold instrument settings in place of a run of 'the supply was set to X' sentences
tables.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template + Appendix A + Week 10 assignment (significant digits)

contents: the Excel model and data tables
the complete source-resistance measurement procedure, with a short description of it in the body
rules: each appendix is referred to from the body
large tables fit the page width rather than splitting across pages
the body summarizes and explains whatever the appendix holds, so a reader who never opens the appendix still follows the report
appendices.delivery: appendices uploaded as a separate PDF alongside the Word report
appendices.source: Stated for the formal report only: instructor template (separate PDF upload) + Appendix A part III.D (raw data, sample calculations) + Week 10 assignment (Excel tables, source-resistance procedure)

voice.person: Appendix A: third person (no I or we) and past tense for what took place, with first person and active voice permitted in some situations, so check with the instructor. The instructor template prefers active voice where possible without I or we, allows we or I only as a last resort, and says staying passive may be best.
voice.tense: Past for procedure, present for discussing results, future for future work; one tense per paragraph.
voice.style: Report what was done. Do not rewrite the lab notebook, and do not write it as step-by-step instructions to the reader.
voice.source: Stated for the formal report only: Appendix A + instructor template

units_and_numbers.significant_digits: set display precision to a reasonable number of significant digits; prefer ordinary notation over scientific when it stays readable
units_and_numbers.source: Stated for the formal report only: Appendix A (proper units with all numerical results) + Week 10 assignment (significant digits)

terminology.software_first_reference: Give the simulator's full trademarked name (Cadence PSpice) on first reference and PSpice after that, not PSPICE, Pspice, or pspice.
terminology.source: Stated for the formal report only: Week 10 assignment

tooling.calculation: Excel for equation-based models and measured-data reduction
tooling.simulation: Cadence PSpice (Schematics) for ideal and realistic circuit models
tooling.writing: Microsoft Word with the equation editor
tooling.source: Stated for the formal report only: Week 9 and Week 10 assignments

submission.draft: A good draft goes to lab the following week for peer review against a rubric, in three printed copies (stapled, name page omitted). The draft is also submitted to Moodle as a Word file. The Rhetoric Center is available before the draft is due.
submission.final: Word report plus an appendices PDF, uploaded together to Moodle. A printed report is stapled, with no paper clips.
submission.individual_work: Measured data may be shared with a lab partner. Graphs, tables, analysis, and prose are individual.
submission.source: Stated for the formal report only: Week 10 assignment (draft, file naming, individual work) + instructor template (final upload) + Appendix A (stapling)

methods.title: Three-way comparison: equation model, simulation, measurement
methods.when: Analog labs that predict a frequency response (resonance, filters, amplifiers) and then measure it.
steps: Measure the actual component values (DMM for R, bridge for L and small C) before modeling.
Build the equation model in Excel from the transfer function, in an ideal version and a realistic one that includes source and parasitic resistances, using the measured values.
Simulate the same ideal and realistic circuits in PSpice and copy the trace data into the spreadsheet.
Measure output amplitude across the sweep, with extra points near the feature of interest (resonance or corner).
Convert every data set to gain on the same basis (V/V or dB = 20 log10 of Vout/Vin).
Before comparing, compute the resonant frequency from the measured L and C and check that every model and the measurement peak or notch near it.
Plot all sets on one log-frequency graph: measured data as markers, models as lines.
Discuss each comparison the assignment enumerates in its own paragraph.
pitfalls: Leaving nominal-value models in the final report after the lab says to use measured values only. Observed in one submission: the equation model used measured values while the simulation still held nominal ones, so their resonances sat several kHz apart while the text called the curves identical.
Taking input amplitude from the function generator display instead of the oscilloscope.
Confusing peak and peak-to-peak amplitude when setting or reading the input.
Several ground points in the circuit, which can short components.
Overlapping traces left unexplained; say so in the text when two models coincide.

methods.title: Function-generator output resistance
methods.when: Any lab where the source's internal resistance enters the realistic model.
steps: Measure the open-circuit output with the oscilloscope.
Load the source with a known measured resistor and measure the loaded voltage.
Solve the voltage divider for the internal resistance: R_src = R_load x (V_open / V_loaded - 1).
Repeat on the specific bench generator in use, because units differ.
Summarize the method in the body and put the full procedure in an appendix.
pitfalls: Reusing a value measured on a different generator.
Reading the open-circuit voltage as peak-to-peak and the loaded voltage as RMS, or the reverse. Both readings must be the same measure or the divider is meaningless.
Re-adjusting the input amplitude after connecting the circuit; set it once, before connecting.

methods.title: Nominal, tolerance range, measured
methods.when: Design labs where component choice drives a performance spec (gain, corner frequency).
steps: Compute the ideal component values from the design equations.
Choose the nearest available nominal values.

Compute the worst-case minimum and maximum performance from the component tolerances, pairing the extremes that push the result furthest each way. The active-filter assignment gives the tolerances: resistors +/-5%, capacitors +/-20%.
Measure the actual components and recompute.
Compare design goal, nominal, tolerance range, simulated, and measured values in one table.
pitfalls: Pairing tolerance extremes the wrong way, so the reported range is too narrow.
Reporting more significant digits than the tolerances justify.

Copying the nominal gain into both the minimum and maximum rows. Gain depends on the resistor ratio, so its extremes come from the largest and smallest ratio the tolerances allow. Observed in one submission.

methods.title: First-order active filter design
steps: Take the filter type, pass-band gain, and corner frequency from the assignment's parameter procedure.

Fix the capacitor, then solve the gain and corner-frequency expressions for the two resistors. The assignment states them: low-pass |H0| = R2/R1 and fc = 1/(2 pi R2 C); high-pass |H0| = R2/R1 and fc = 1/(2 pi R1 C).
Carry through the tolerance-range method.
Simulate the nominal and actual circuits with the simple op-amp model, then read the pass-band gain and the frequency where gain falls to 0.707 of it.
Build and measure the circuit, and plot the simulated traces as lines with the measured points as markers.
pitfalls: Reversing the op-amp supply rails, which can destroy the part.
Expecting the simple op-amp model to show high-frequency roll-off; it does not, unlike the detailed 741 model.

Putting gain in dB in a column headed V/V, as one submission's gain-bandwidth table did. Say which unit the column holds, convert with dB = 20 log10 of the ratio, and take the gain-bandwidth product from the V/V value.

assignment_families.title: Formal analog lab report
stages: pre-lab (Week 9): equations typeset in Word, equation and PSpice models with nominal values, turned in printed at the start of the next lab
lab: measure components and the frequency response
good draft taken to peer review
deliverables: Word report: title page, abstract page, numbered sections
appendices PDF: model tables, simulation data, measured data, procedures
what_good_looks_like: The abstract summarizes the experiments and the findings in one short paragraph, up to about eight sentences, with no figure references and no detailed numbers.

The introduction gives a reader with the same training what they need to follow the analysis: the goals, then the background theory, equations, and diagrams of the system. The assignment requires the PSpice circuit diagrams to be pasted into the body; where they sit in the introduction is the author's choice.

The results graphs overlay the five traces the assignment names (measured, simulation ideal, simulation realistic, equation ideal, equation realistic) on a log axis, with markers for data, lines for models, and a legend.
Only measured component values feed the models in the report. The nominal-value pre-lab runs are left out, and Cadence PSpice is named in full on first mention.

The analysis gives at least a paragraph to each comparison the Week 10 assignment lists: series against parallel behavior, calculated against measured resonant frequency, models against measurements, ideal against realistic models, and the two modeling methods (Excel equations against PSpice). Each names where error crept in, how significant it was, and whether a procedural change would remove it.
The models are compared on more than accuracy, for example simplicity or cost, because the template asks whether other factors should influence the choice of a model.
The equipment section says why each instrument was needed, not only what it was.
The conclusion ties the results back to the stated goals and suggests follow-up work.
Appendices are referenced from the body, and each data table fits on its page.
assignment_families.basis: the Week 10 lab assignment (instructor-written, with its report steps and Appendix A, the Engineering Department Report Standards) and the instructor's report template, which the assignment says gives essential instructions. The template file found is a student-saved copy (metadata 2025-04-08, one revision, one minute of editing) with no student content; its guidance sentences appear word for word in a second, partly student-written file, and its placeholders, company field, and text point to the instructor, but it cannot be shown to be byte-identical to the original. A file in the iCloud term folder named as the SP24 template is not the template: it is a student's draft saved over it, with only its introduction and closing guidance pages left as template text, and no rule rests on its student pages. The one completed formal report found is a student's own, written in a complaint register and not shown to have been submitted (a near-identical copy is named as the assignment prescribes, but no submission or grade exists), so it supports layout only and is not a model of prose.

assignment_families.title: Short-form lab report (op-amp and filter design labs)
deliverables: a short report built on the instructor's Moodle template and following the assignment's report list; the op-amp assignment asks for two pages if possible
what_good_looks_like: Name, lab section, and date of the experiment filled in (the op-amp assignment's first item).
The measured component values, and for the op-amp lab a short section on what the input increase showed about the op-amp rails.
The assignment's table filled completely, with units and sensible digits. The op-amp gain-bandwidth table uses gains in V/V, never dB, and is followed by a description of what the data show.
One graph with simulated traces as lines (different line types, no markers) and measured points as markers with no connecting lines, with axis titles and a legend.

The PSpice circuit diagram as a screen capture, and the measured and simulated data copied from the spreadsheet without the graph, with a sensible number of significant digits and text no smaller than 8 pt if the table is shrunk to fit.

For the filter design lab: the equations for the resistor values entered with the equation editor, and a sentence or two comparing each result with the design goals. Partners may share the design and data through step 6, and each student writes step 7 and submits the full report to Moodle individually.
assignment_families.basis: the op-amp and active-filter lab assignments (instructor-written; they list the report contents, and each says a report template with placeholders is on Moodle). The blank templates were not found in the seven iCloud term folders or in OneDrive, so typography and page layout are unspecified. Two student reports appear to be filled-in copies (their file metadata credits the instructor, and the filter report's comparison-table rows cite the assignment's own step numbers), so their header fields, section labels, and table rows are probably the instructor's with moderate confidence, but nothing states which text was original. All prose in them is the student's, is informal, and contains errors listed under methods, so they support layout only.

assignment_families.title: Weekly digital-logic turn-in worksheet
stages: complete the fill-in handout page during the lab (truth tables, Karnaugh maps, expressions, timing diagrams, or state tables, by week)
build and simulate the design in Quartus, then program the device and test it on the breadboard
have the instructor or lab assistant sign off the working circuit when the week's handout calls for it
assemble the hand-in the way that week's handout says, on paper or on Moodle as the instructor directs
deliverables: the completed fill-in page (the self-test pages carry a Name line)
the attachments that week's hand-in line names, such as an Excel truth table, minimization work, a state table, a Quartus schematic, and Quartus simulation waveforms
what_good_looks_like: Every blank on the handout page is filled in: truth tables, the Karnaugh map, the simplified expression, and the circuit drawn in the box provided.

The hand-in matches that week's own hand-in line, which differs by week. Weeks 3 and 6 want the schematic and the simulation waveforms with the minimization work; week 5 wants a printed state table, minimization work, and schematic and says the simulation printout is not needed; the week 2 self-test wants the Excel truth table, the minimization work, the Quartus schematic, and the simulation; week 4 part 2 wants the completed page and the simulation waveforms.
Quartus schematics and simulations are copied into one Word document with snip or print screen, and the number of sheets is kept down by putting several items on one sheet.

A working circuit is demonstrated to the instructor or lab assistant for sign-off (weeks 3, 5, and 6). The handouts also ask for two earlier check-ins: week 1 says to show the completed work to the instructor or lab assistant before moving on to week 2, and week 6 asks for the state table to be reviewed before the design continues. In one archived handout the sign-off appears as initials beside the printed sign-off step; otherwise it leaves no document.

Partners: a partner may share the final verification step when the two designs are identical (week 3). In week 6 partners submit identical files with both names stated and the sequence they worked on identified.
Where a handout says there is nothing to turn in (the week 2 tool exercise), nothing is turned in, and the instructor may give specific instructions on how to submit.
assignment_families.basis: the printed instructor text of the weekly handouts and turn-in pages for weeks 1 to 6, each of which carries its own hand-in line (hundreds to a few thousand extractable characters per turn-in file). The students' answers on those pages have no text layer, so the text pass recorded structure and conventions only, with no problem content and no values. The handouts carry copyright years from 2023 to 2025, so a handout can predate the term it was used in. No handout was found for weeks 7 and 11 in the iCloud term folder; the analog weeks are covered by the other two families. The weekly handout PDFs themselves carry the student's answers in ink; those were read as page images and are recorded under observed_practice.

observed_practice.medium: Answers are written in digital ink directly on the lab handout PDF: tables filled cell by cell, expressions on the printed answer lines, circuits drawn in the printed boxes, output waveforms drawn on the printed timing axes, and gate names labelled on the printed figures.
observed_practice.minimization: Karnaugh-map groupings are drawn as coloured loops or rectangles, and each product term of the resulting expression is written in the colour of its group.

The handouts describe a separate Word document; whether this PDF or such a document was what was handed in is not shown.

magnitudes.quantity: function-generator output resistance from the open-circuit and loaded voltage method
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: bench function generators are built with a 50 ohm output, and the one measurement seen, in a student's Spring 2025 lab notes, was about 52 ohm. The bounds are a margin around 50.
magnitudes.note: Near zero or in the hundreds: the open-circuit and loaded readings were swapped, or one was peak-to-peak and the other RMS. A loaded reading larger than the open-circuit reading is impossible. Measure it on the generator in use. A generator that is not a 50 ohm design would fall outside this range legitimately.

magnitudes.quantity: voltage gain at resonance of the realistic series RLC circuit, output taken across the resistor
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: a passive network cannot amplify, and the realistic model's peak is R / (R + R_src + coil resistance), a few tenths of a dB to a couple of dB below unity for a resistor of a few hundred ohms against a source of about 50 ohm. The ideal model's peak is exactly 1.
magnitudes.note: Above 1: the input amplitude was read from the generator display instead of the oscilloscope, or peak and peak-to-peak were mixed. A negative number, such as -1.3, is a gain in dB entered as V/V. Below 0.5 is possible only when the resistor is comparable to the source resistance, which is not this circuit.

magnitudes.quantity: gain-bandwidth product of an inverting op-amp stage built on a 741-type op amp
magnitudes.basis: Physical plausibility, not a course rule: a 741-type op amp has a unity-gain bandwidth near 1 MHz, and pass-band gain times corner frequency stays near it across gain settings. A student's Spring 2025 op-amp report lists roughly 0.9 to 1.0 MHz simulated and 0.6 to 0.7 MHz on the bench.
magnitudes.note: Too high: the gain was left in dB where V/V is needed. A 13 dB stage then gives 13 in place of about 4.6, roughly 3 times too high, but a 33 dB stage gives 33 in place of about 46, which stays inside this range, so read the column heading and not only the range. Off by 1000: the corner was multiplied in kHz as if it were Hz. The simple op-amp model has no roll-off and gives no corner, so this applies only to the detailed 741 model.
